usage: 존댓말, neutral-polite; the default way anyone answers a call
반말-ish flat tone to a close friend whose number you saw; still the same word
More formal/businesslike; 네 first then 여보세요 at work or with strangers
Natural extension to test a silent or weak line mid-call
examples: 여보세요?
Hello?
The bare one-word answer the moment your phone rings
여보세요, 김민수 씨 휴대폰 맞으세요?
Hello, is this Kim Minsu's phone?
Everyday use: checking you reached the right person
여보세요? 여보세요? 소리가 자꾸 끊겨요.
Hello? Hello? You keep cutting out.
Fuller situation: repeating it while a bad line drops in and out
nuance: 여보세요 is the dedicated telephone 'hello' and is almost never used face to face — said to someone in front of you it sounds like a joke or like snapping a daydreamer awake ('hello? anyone home?'). It comes from 여기 보세요 ('look here'), a call for attention, which is why it doubles as a mid-call line check. The in-person greeting is 안녕하세요, and the two are not swappable: 안녕하세요 asks after wellbeing, while 여보세요 just opens the voice channel. Register sits at neutral-polite (the 세요 ending), fine for strangers, elders, and customer service alike; do not clip it to 여보, which now means 'honey/darling' between spouses. The classic English-speaker error is using 여보세요 like 'hi' when meeting people — keep it strictly for phones.

Shortening it to 여보 to sound casual — 여보 alone means 'dear/honey' between a married couple, so it is bizarre to a stranger; keep the full 여보세요.
Translating 'hello, this is John' as 여보세요, 존이에요 and stopping — after 여보세요 Koreans usually add 안녕하세요 or 저 ...인데요 to introduce themselves.

english: Is now a good time to talk?
usage: 존댓말; polite check to an elder, boss, or anyone you respect
반말 to a close friend or younger person
Would it be possible to talk now?
More formal/격식; business calls or a first call to a stranger
Do you have a minute to talk?
Extension with 잠깐 signalling you will be brief
examples: 여보세요, 지금 통화 괜찮으세요?
Hello, is now a good time to talk?
The standard opener right after the other person picks up
팀장님, 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? 잠깐 보고드릴 게 있어서요.
Sir, is now okay to talk? I have something brief to report.
Everyday work use: checking before launching into business
지금 통화 괜찮으세요? 혹시 운전 중이시면 이따 다시 걸게요.
Is now a good time? If you're driving, I'll call back later.
Fuller situation: offering to call back if they are busy
nuance: 지금 통화 괜찮으세요? is the courteous way to check the other person is free before you start talking — Korean phone etiquette treats launching straight into business without asking as slightly rude, especially with elders, clients, or a boss. 통화 means 'a phone call' specifically, so this is not interchangeable with face-to-face 지금 시간 괜찮으세요? ('do you have time now?'); the dividing line is that 통화 names the medium. To go casual, drop to 통화 괜찮아? with a friend; to go formal, use 통화 가능하실까요?, which sounds more deferential and businesslike. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'can you talk?' as 말할 수 있어요?, which literally asks whether the person is physically able to speak — wrong and slightly bizarre; the idiom is built on 통화, not 말하다.

Dropping 지금 in a context that needs it — without 지금 it can sound like a general request; add 지금 to mean 'right now.'
Using flat 통화 괜찮아? with a boss or client — that is 반말; raise it to 괜찮으세요? or 가능하실까요?.

usage: 존댓말; standard polite 'who's calling' on an unknown number
반말; only with a close friend whose unsaved number called you
More formal/격식; business desks and reception
Extension; 실례지만 softens the direct identity question
examples: 여보세요? 누구세요?
Hello? Who's calling?
The basic pairing when you don't recognize the number
죄송하지만 누구세요? 잘 못 들었어요.
Sorry, who is this? I didn't catch it.
Everyday follow-up when a name came through unclearly
누구세요? 어디라고 하셨죠? 성함 좀 말씀해 주시겠어요?
Who is this? Where did you say you're from? Could you give your name?
Fuller situation: at a desk pinning down an unidentified caller
nuance: 누구세요? politely asks a caller's identity — 누구 ('who') plus honorific 이세요 — so it honors the unknown person while you find out who they are. The key contrast is against 누구야? and 누구냐?, which are 반말/blunt and sound suspicious or hostile ('who the heck are you?'), fine only with close friends. For business politeness Koreans upgrade to 누구시죠? or 어디세요? (literally 'where are you from?', i.e. which company), the norm on work calls; the dividing line is that 어디세요? asks for the affiliation, not the personal name. Watch the particle trap: it stands alone, so never add 가/이 (누구가세요 is wrong). Another pitfall is answering with 누구세요? on a call you placed — the caller introduces themselves first (저 ...인데요); 누구세요? is for when you RECEIVE a call from someone unknown.

Adding a subject particle: 누구가세요/누구이세요 is wrong — it is simply 누구 + 세요.

usage: 존댓말; asking anyone to hold the line briefly
반말; to a close friend or younger person
Could you hold for a moment?
One moment, I'll put them right on.
Extension; holding to transfer the call to someone else
examples: 잠시만요.
One moment.
The bare phrase as you set the phone down to check something
잠시만요, 펜 좀 가져올게요.
Hold on, let me grab a pen.
Everyday use: pausing to write down what they're saying
잠시만요, 담당자 연결해 드리겠습니다. 끊지 말고 기다려 주세요.
One moment, I'll connect you to the right person. Please don't hang up.
Fuller situation: a call-center transfer with a 'don't hang up' note
nuance: 잠시만요 means 'just a moment' and is the all-purpose 'hold on' on the phone, at a counter, or to slip past someone in a crowd. On a call it tells the other person you are stepping away briefly without ending the conversation. 잠시 is slightly more formal than the everyday 잠깐, but 잠시만요/잠깐만요 are interchangeable in practice; the 반말 form is 잠깐만 (or 잠시만), dropping the polite 요. The dividing line with 기다려 주세요 ('please wait') is length and tone: 잠시만요 is a quick, almost reflexive 'sec', while 기다려 주세요 is a fuller, more explicit request. The English-speaker error is reaching for a literal 'wait' as 기다리세요, which sounds like a command ('you, wait!'); the natural, softening idiom is 잠시만요, and the polite request form adds 주시겠어요?.

Saying 잠깐만 to a customer or elder — it is 반말; use 잠시만요 or the fuller 잠시만 기다려 주세요.
Spelling/spacing it as 잠시 만요 — it is one chunk, 잠시만요, with 만요 attached.

usage: 존댓말; politely telling a stranger they misdialed
반말; to a friend who called you by mistake
I believe you have the wrong number.
More formal/격식; softened with 같습니다 at work or to elders
여기 그런 사람 없는데요. 전화 잘못 거셨어요.
There's no one here by that name. Wrong number.
Extension; explaining before saying they misdialed
examples: 아, 전화 잘못 거셨어요.
Oh, you've got the wrong number.
The bare reply when a stranger asks for someone unknown
죄송한데 전화 잘못 거신 것 같아요. 몇 번에 거셨어요?
Sorry, I think you have the wrong number. What number did you dial?
Everyday use: gently checking which number they meant
여보세요? 김 과장님이요? 여기 그런 분 안 계세요. 전화 잘못 거신 것 같은데요.
Hello? Manager Kim? There's no one here by that name. I think you misdialed.
Fuller situation: a misdirected call at an office
nuance: 전화 잘못 거셨어요 tells a caller they reached the wrong number — 잘못 ('wrongly') plus 걸다 ('to place/hang a call'), in the honorific past 거셨어요. The verb for dialing is 걸다 (전화를 걸다), so 'I called' is 전화 걸었어요 and 'you misdialed' is 잘못 거셨어요; do not use 하다 here for the act of dialing. Softening matters: bare 전화 잘못 거셨어요 can sound curt, so Koreans cushion it with 죄송한데 or hedge with ...것 같아요 ('seems like'). The 반말 form is 잘못 걸었어 to a friend. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'wrong number' as 틀린 번호 — 틀리다 means 'to be incorrect/mistaken (as a fact)', so 틀린 번호 sounds like the number itself is faulty; the idiom is the adverb 잘못 with the verb 걸다, describing the action of dialing wrongly.

Using 전화 잘못 했어요 — dialing uses 걸다, not 하다; say 잘못 거셨어요/잘못 걸었어요.
Delivering it flatly to a stranger — add 죄송한데 or ...것 같아요 so it doesn't sound annoyed.

usage: 존댓말; telling anyone the line is bad
반말; to a close friend or younger person
More formal/격식; -는데요 sounds gentler and more polite
소리가 잘 안 들려요. 좀 크게 말씀해 주시겠어요?
I can't hear well. Could you speak up a bit?
Extension; asking them to speak louder
examples: 여보세요? 잘 안 들려요.
Hello? I can't hear you.
The bare phrase the moment the line goes faint
죄송한데 잘 안 들려요. 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?
Sorry, I can't hear well. Could you say that again?
Everyday use: asking for a repeat because of the connection
여기 지하라서 그런지 잘 안 들려요. 밖으로 나가서 다시 걸게요.
Maybe because I'm underground, I can't hear you. Let me step out and call back.
Fuller situation: explaining the cause and offering to redial
nuance: 잘 안 들려요 reports that the other person's voice is faint — 들리다 is the intransitive 'to be heard/audible', so the sound is the subject, not you. This is the right verb: 듣다 ('to listen') would wrongly imply you are choosing not to listen, while 들리다 means the audio itself isn't coming through. Keep the order 잘 안 들려요 ('well-not-audible'); 안 잘 들려요 is ungrammatical. To go gentler/more formal, use 잘 안 들리는데요; the 반말 is 잘 안 들려. The nearest alternative is 소리가 작아요 ('the volume is low'), but that blames the volume specifically, whereas 잘 안 들려요 covers any reason — static, dropout, noise. The English-speaker trap is 당신을 못 들어요 ('I can't hear you'), which uses 듣다 with a person object and sounds like a personal refusal; native phrasing makes the sound, not the person, the subject.

Confusing it with 못 알아들어요 ('I can't understand') — that is about comprehension; for a bad line use 잘 안 들려요.

usage: 존댓말; reporting a dropped call to anyone
More formal/격식; 통화 and -네요 sound a touch more composed
The call suddenly dropped a moment ago.
Extension; explaining a drop when you reconnect
examples: 여보세요? 아, 아까 전화가 끊겼네요.
Hello? Oh, the call dropped earlier.
The bare phrase when you call back after a drop
미안해요, 전화가 끊겼어요. 터널을 지나가서 그랬나 봐요.
Sorry, the call dropped. Must've been the tunnel.
Everyday use: apologizing and guessing the cause
방금 통화하다가 전화가 끊겨서 다시 걸었어요. 어디까지 얘기했죠?
The call cut out mid-conversation so I called back. Where were we?
Fuller situation: resuming after redialing
nuance: 전화가 끊겼어요 says the call ended unintentionally — 끊기다 is the passive/intransitive of 끊다 ('to cut'), so the call 'got cut off' on its own. This is the dividing line learners miss: 전화를 끊었어요 (active 끊다 with object particle 를) means 'I hung up on purpose', while 전화가 끊겼어요 (passive 끊기다 with subject particle 가) means 'it dropped'. Choosing the wrong voice flips the meaning from an accident to a deliberate hang-up — potentially rude. To soften or sound more formal, 통화가 끊어졌어요 works; the 반말 is 전화 끊겼어. The nearest neighbor 전화 끊을게요 is unrelated in meaning ('I'll hang up now'), a polite sign-off, so don't confuse 끊다 (deliberate) with 끊기다 (accidental). The English-speaker trap is using 끊었어요 for an accidental drop, which sounds like you cut them off yourself.

Confusing it with 끊을게요 ('I'll hang up') — that announces ending the call on purpose, not a dropout.

usage: 존댓말; promising to call back, neutral-polite
반말; to a close friend or younger person
More formal/격식; humble 드리다 for a client, boss, or elder
I'll call you back in a bit.
Extension; 이따가 pins it to later today
examples: 지금 좀 바빠서요, 다시 전화할게요.
I'm a bit busy now, I'll call you back.
The bare promise when you can't talk right now
회의 끝나고 다시 전화할게요. 한 시간쯤 뒤에요.
I'll call back after my meeting, in about an hour.
Everyday use: giving a rough time for the callback
지금 운전 중이라 다시 전화할게요. 도착하면 바로 연락드릴게요.
I'm driving, so I'll call you back. I'll reach out as soon as I arrive.
Fuller situation: explaining why and committing to a follow-up
nuance: 다시 전화할게요 is a promise that YOU will phone again — the -ㄹ게요 ending specifically marks the speaker's own intention/commitment, which is why it fits a personal promise and would be wrong for asking someone else to act. 다시 means 'again', so the whole thing is 'I'll call again.' To raise politeness toward a boss or client, swap 전화하다 for the humble 전화드리다 → 다시 전화드릴게요/전화드리겠습니다; the 반말 is 다시 전화할게. The nearest alternative 다시 걸게요 uses 걸다 (the dialing verb) and is equally natural; the difference is negligible. The English-speaker trap is 'call you back' producing 당신을 다시 불러요 — 부르다 means 'to call out to / summon' a person physically, not to telephone; the phone verb is 전화하다/전화 걸다, and you do not insert 당신을.

Adding 당신을 — 전화하다 doesn't take a person as object that way; just say 다시 전화할게요.

usage: 존댓말; voicemail prompt or asking a caller to leave word

english: Shall we set up a time to meet?

More formal/격식; suggesting to a client or senior
